2019-Q1.shortcut: Match each scale to its recommended summary: nominal - mode, bar/pie; ordinal - median; interval/ratio - mean and SD, histogram. Statement 1 pairs the median with the RATIO scale, where the mean is recommended, so it fails. Statements 2 and 3 are correct.
tips: Learn the scale-to-statistic table once: nominal gives mode, frequency, bar and pie; ordinal gives median, quartiles; interval and ratio give mean, SD and histogram.
The permissible/recommended distinction is what the examiner exploits. The median is PERMISSIBLE at ratio level but the mean is RECOMMENDED there, because the ratio scale carries more information.

Pie charts require categories that partition a whole, so they suit nominal data; histograms require a continuous numeric axis, so they suit interval/ratio data. Never draw a histogram of nominal categories.
Standard deviation needs equal intervals to be meaningful, which is exactly why it is recommended from the interval scale upwards and not for ordinal data.
solution: Statement 1: the median is the recommended measure of location for ORDINAL data, but for ratio-scale data the arithmetic mean is recommended because the scale supports addition and ratios. Pairing the median with the ratio scale is therefore not the recommended choice. FALSE.
Statement 2: nominal data consist of unordered categories with frequencies; the standard displays are bar diagrams and pie diagrams. TRUE.
Statement 3: interval-scale data are numeric with equal intervals, so a histogram is the appropriate graph and the standard deviation is the appropriate measure of variability. TRUE.
Only statements 2 and 3 are correct.
Hence option (b) is correct.

2019-Q2.shortcut: X takes only 0 and 1, so X^r = X for every r and E(X^r) = P(X=1) = a3 + a4. XY takes the values 0, -1, +1, so E(XY) = a4 - a3 and (XY)^(2n) is 1 exactly when X = 1, giving a3 + a4. All three hold.
tips: Indicator trick: a variable taking only 0 and 1 satisfies X^r = X for all r >= 1, so all its moments coincide with its mean. That settles statement 1 with no algebra.
Build the value table of XY before touching statement 3: XY = 0 on the whole X = 0 row, XY = -1 with probability a3 and XY = +1 with probability a4.
An EVEN power kills the sign, so (XY)^(2n) equals 1 whenever XY is non-zero. Hence its expectation is P(XY not 0) = a3 + a4, the same as statement 1's answer - a nice internal consistency check.
When several statements about the same tiny table all reduce to the row/column sums, expect 'all of them' - but verify the one with the sign, here statement 2.
solution: The table gives P(X=0, Y=-1) = a1, P(X=0, Y=1) = a2, P(X=1, Y=-1) = a3, P(X=1, Y=1) = a4.
Statement 1: X takes only the values 0 and 1, so X^r = X for every r >= 1. Hence E(X^r) = E(X) = 0(a1 + a2) + 1(a3 + a4) = a3 + a4. TRUE.
Statement 3: the product XY takes the value 0 with probability a1 + a2, the value -1 with probability a3, and +1 with probability a4.
Raising to the even power 2n maps 0 to 0 and both -1 and +1 to 1, so E[(XY)^(2n)] = a3 + a4 for every n. TRUE.
All three statements are correct, option (d).

2019-Q3.shortcut: Different units force a RELATIVE comparison. CV(height) = 6.5/115 = 5.65% and CV(weight) = 2.7/23 = 11.74%. The ratio is 11.74/5.65 = 2.08, so weight is about twice as variable.
tips: Whenever two variables have different units (cm and kg), never compare standard deviations directly - compute the coefficient of variation, CV = s/mean.
Estimate the ratio mentally: 2.7/23 is a little over 11% while 6.5/115 is a little under 6%. Roughly 11 against 6 is about 2, which selects option (b) without a calculator.
The CV is dimensionless precisely so that such comparisons are legitimate; it is also the reason the answer is a pure number with no units.
Options (c) and (d) invert the comparison. Fix in your mind which variable is the SUBJECT of the sentence ('variable in body weight') before choosing.
solution: Because height is in centimetres and weight in kilograms, the two standard deviations cannot be compared directly; we use the coefficient of variation CV = (s/mean) x 100%.
For body height: CV1 = (6.5/115) x 100 = 5.65%.
For body weight: CV2 = (2.7/23) x 100 = 11.74%.
The ratio CV2/CV1 = 11.74/5.65 = 2.08, which is approximately 2.
Hence the boys are about twice as variable in body weight as in body height.
Option (b) is correct.

2019-Q4.shortcut: Under independence the expected (AB) is (A)(B)/N = 50 x 60/100 = 30. The observed 40 exceeds 30, so A and B are positively associated.
tips: The whole test is one comparison: observed (AB) against (A)(B)/N. Greater means positive association, smaller means negative, equal means independence.
Compute (A)(B)/N first and keep it as a single number - here 30 - then a one-glance comparison with 40 finishes the item.
Yule's Q would confirm the sign: the 2x2 table is (AB)=40, (A beta)=10, (alpha B)=20, (alpha beta)=30, so ad - bc = 1200 - 200 > 0, again positive.
Option (d) is a trap for candidates who think a 2x2 table is insufficient - it is entirely sufficient, since the four cell frequencies follow from (A), (B), (AB) and N.
solution: For two attributes A and B, independence means (AB) = (A)(B)/N.
Here (A) = 50, (B) = 60 and N = 100, so the expected frequency under independence is (50)(60)/100 = 30.
The observed frequency is (AB) = 40, which is greater than 30.
Since the observed joint frequency exceeds the frequency expected under independence, the attributes are positively associated.
As a check, the full table is (AB) = 40, (A beta) = 10, (alpha B) = 20, (alpha beta) = 30, giving Yule's Q = (1200 - 200)/(1200 + 200) = 5/7 > 0.
Hence option (b) is correct.

2019-Q5.shortcut: b_xy = 4 from the first line and b_yx = k from the second. Since r^2 = b_xy b_yx must lie in [0,1], we need 0 <= 4k <= 1, i.e. 0 <= k <= 1/4.
tips: Read the regression coefficients straight off: in x = 4y + 5 the coefficient of y is b_xy = 4; in y = kx + 4 the coefficient of x is b_yx = k.
The master constraint is r^2 = b_xy . b_yx with 0 <= r^2 <= 1. Every 'which values are possible' regression item reduces to this inequality.
Both regression coefficients must share the sign of r, so with b_xy = 4 > 0 we need k > 0 - that alone eliminates options (b) and (c).
The geometric mean of the two regression coefficients is |r|; here sqrt(4k) <= 1 gives the same bound in one step.
solution: The line of regression of x on y is x = b_xy . y + constant, so from x = 4y + 5 we read b_xy = 4.
The line of regression of y on x is y = b_yx . x + constant, so from y = kx + 4 we read b_yx = k.
The fundamental relation is r^2 = b_xy . b_yx = 4k.
Since r is a correlation coefficient, 0 <= r^2 <= 1, so 0 <= 4k <= 1.
Dividing by 4: 0 <= k <= 1/4.
Hence option (d) is correct.

2019-Q6.shortcut: a = r s_Y/s_X and c = r s_X/s_Y. Multiplying gives ac = r^2, so r = sqrt(ac); dividing gives c/a = (s_X/s_Y)^2, so s_X/s_Y = sqrt(c/a).
tips: Two moves only: MULTIPLY the regression coefficients to isolate r, DIVIDE them to isolate the ratio of standard deviations. Every question of this type uses that pair.
Keep the subscripts straight: b_YX = a = r s_Y/s_X carries s_Y on top, while b_XY = c = r s_X/s_Y carries s_X on top. Getting these the wrong way round turns (a) into (d).
The intercepts b and d carry no information about r or the standard deviations - they only locate the means. Option (c), which uses bd, is therefore impossible.
Since c/a = s_X^2/s_Y^2, the ratio s_X/s_Y is sqrt(c/a) - note it is c over a, not a over c, which is the sole difference between options (a) and (d).
solution: The regression of Y on X is Y = aX + b, so its slope is the regression coefficient b_YX = a = r (s_Y/s_X).
The regression of X on Y is X = cY + d, so its slope is b_XY = c = r (s_X/s_Y).
Multiplying: ac = r^2 (s_Y/s_X)(s_X/s_Y) = r^2, hence r = sqrt(ac) (taking the sign common to a and c).
Dividing: c/a = [r s_X/s_Y] / [r s_Y/s_X] = (s_X/s_Y)^2.
Therefore s_X/s_Y = sqrt(c/a).
The pair is (sqrt(ac), sqrt(c/a)), option (a).

2019-Q7.shortcut: Cov(X+tZ, Y+tZ) = t^2 and each variance is 1 + t^2, so rho = t^2/(1+t^2) = 0.25. Cross-multiplying, 4t^2 = 1 + t^2 gives t^2 = 1/3 and |t| = 1/sqrt3.
tips: The shared component Z is what creates the correlation: only the Z-terms survive in the covariance because X, Y, Z are independent.
The form rho = t^2/(1 + t^2) is the standard 'common factor' correlation; note that it is always in [0,1) and increases in |t|, so a small rho means a small |t|.
Invert quickly: rho = t^2/(1+t^2) rearranges to t^2 = rho/(1 - rho) = 0.25/0.75 = 1/3. Memorise that inversion - it saves the whole cross-multiplication.
Only |theta| is asked because rho depends on theta^2; both +1/sqrt3 and -1/sqrt3 give correlation 0.25.
solution: Let U = X + theta Z and V = Y + theta Z, with X, Y, Z independent standard normal.
Var(U) = Var(X) + theta^2 Var(Z) = 1 + theta^2, and similarly Var(V) = 1 + theta^2.
Cov(U, V) = Cov(X, Y) + theta Cov(X, Z) + theta Cov(Z, Y) + theta^2 Var(Z) = 0 + 0 + 0 + theta^2 = theta^2.
Therefore rho = theta^2/(1 + theta^2).
Setting theta^2/(1 + theta^2) = 0.25 gives 4 theta^2 = 1 + theta^2, so 3 theta^2 = 1 and theta^2 = 1/3.
Hence |theta| = 1/sqrt(3), option (b).

2019-Q8.shortcut: The expression is Fisher's z-transformation, z = (1/2) log[(1+r)/(1-r)] = arctanh(r). Its asymptotic variance is 1/(n-3).
tips: Fisher's z: mean approximately (1/2)log[(1+rho)/(1-rho)] and variance exactly 1/(n-3). The variance is FREE of rho - that is the entire point of the transformation.
Do not confuse it with the null-case test statistic r sqrt(n-2)/sqrt(1-r^2) ~ t with n-2 d.f., which is where the tempting 1/(n-2) in option (c) comes from.
Use z when testing rho = rho0 for a non-zero rho0, or when comparing two independent correlations; use the t-statistic only for rho = 0.
Remember the pairing 'z goes with n-3' as a fixed unit; the confidence interval for rho is built by transforming, adding +-1.96/sqrt(n-3), and transforming back.
solution: The statistic (1/2) log_e[(1+r)/(1-r)] is Fisher's z-transformation of the sample correlation coefficient, equal to arctanh(r).
For samples from a bivariate normal population with correlation rho, z is approximately normally distributed even for moderate n.
Its asymptotic mean is (1/2) log_e[(1+rho)/(1-rho)] = arctanh(rho).
Its asymptotic variance is 1/(n - 3), which notably does not depend on rho - this variance-stabilising property is the reason for the transformation.
Hence the variance is 1/(n-3), option (d).

2019-Q9.shortcut: The four points satisfy Y = X - 1 exactly, so r = +1 > 0. But X^2 = 1, 0, 1, 4 against Y^2 = 4, 1, 0, 1 - as X^2 rises Y^2 broadly falls, and the covariance works out to -0.25 per point, so s < 0.
tips: Check for an exact linear relation first: Y = X - 1 here, which forces r = +1 with no arithmetic at all.
Squaring destroys linearity when the data straddle zero. Both X and Y take negative values, so the squares reverse the order of some pairs - that is why the sign can flip.
Compute the covariance of X^2 and Y^2 by deviations: both have mean 1.5, giving deviations (-0.5,-1.5,-0.5,2.5) and (2.5,-0.5,-1.5,-0.5) whose products sum to -1. Negative sum, negative s.
Moral: r measures LINEAR association only; a perfect linear relation between X and Y implies nothing about the correlation between their squares.
solution: The observations are (-1,-2), (0,-1), (1,0), (2,1). Each satisfies Y = X - 1 exactly.
A perfect increasing linear relation gives r = +1, so r > 0.
Now form the squares: X^2 = 1, 0, 1, 4 and Y^2 = 4, 1, 0, 1.
Both sets have mean (1+0+1+4)/4 = 1.5. Deviations of X^2: -0.5, -1.5, -0.5, 2.5. Deviations of Y^2: 2.5, -0.5, -1.5, -0.5.
Sum of products of deviations: (-0.5)(2.5) + (-1.5)(-0.5) + (-0.5)(-1.5) + (2.5)(-0.5) = -1.25 + 0.75 + 0.75 - 1.25 = -1.0, so the covariance is negative and s < 0.
Therefore r > 0 but s < 0, option (a).

2019-Q10.shortcut: r = Cov/(s_X s_Y) gives 0.6 = 4.8/(3 s_Y), so 3 s_Y = 8 and s_Y = 8/3 = 2.67.
tips: Rearranged form worth memorising: s_Y = Cov/(r . s_X). One substitution and you are done.
Take the square root of the variance first: Var(X) = 9 gives s_X = 3, not 9. Using 9 directly yields 0.89 and no matching option.
The arithmetic is clean: 4.8/0.6 = 8, then 8/3 = 2.67. Look for such cancellations before reaching for a calculator.
Consistency check: with s_Y = 8/3, Cov = r s_X s_Y = 0.6 x 3 x 2.667 = 4.8, matching the datum exactly.
solution: The correlation coefficient is defined by r = Cov(X,Y)/(s_X s_Y).
Given Var(X) = 9, the standard deviation is s_X = 3.
Substituting the known values: 0.6 = 4.8/(3 s_Y).
Therefore 3 s_Y = 4.8/0.6 = 8.
Hence option (d) is correct.

2019-Q11.shortcut: Buffon's needle with needle length L and line spacing d (L < d) gives P = 2L/(pi d). With L = l and d = 2l, P = 2l/(2 pi l) = 1/pi.
tips: Buffon's formula: P = 2L/(pi d), valid when the needle is shorter than the gap. Memorise it as 'two L over pi d'.
The lengths cancel whenever d is a fixed multiple of L, so the answer is a pure number - here 1/pi. Expect pi in the denominator of any Buffon answer.
The classical case d = L gives P = 2/pi, which is the historical Monte Carlo estimate of pi. Doubling the spacing halves the probability to 1/pi - a useful sanity check.
Derivation sketch: the distance from the centre to the nearest line is uniform on (0, d/2) and the angle is uniform on (0, pi/2); integrating the intersection condition gives the formula.
solution: This is Buffon's needle problem. Let the stick have length L = l and let the parallel lines be d = 2l apart, so L < d.
Let x be the distance from the centre of the stick to the nearest line, uniform on (0, d/2), and let theta be the acute angle the stick makes with the lines, uniform on (0, pi/2), independently.
The stick crosses a line exactly when x <= (L/2) sin theta.
P = (integral over theta of (L/2) sin theta d theta) / [(d/2)(pi/2)] = [(L/2)(1)] / [(pi d)/4] = 2L/(pi d).
Substituting L = l and d = 2l: P = 2l/(pi . 2l) = 1/pi.
Hence option (c) is correct.

2019-Q12.shortcut: Firing rates 9 : 10 give priors 9/19 and 10/19; the 19s cancel in Bayes' formula. So the answer is (9)(0.7)/[(9)(0.7) + (10)(0.6)] = 6.3/12.3 = 21/41.
tips: When priors come from a ratio, keep them as raw counts (9 and 10) - the common denominator cancels top and bottom and saves all the fraction work.
Multiply counts by hit rates to get 'effective hits': 9 x 0.7 = 6.3 from A1 and 10 x 0.6 = 6.0 from A2. The posterior is just 6.3/(6.3 + 6.0).
Simplify 63/123 by dividing by 3 to reach 21/41 - option (a) 20/41 is the near-miss planted for arithmetic slips.
Plausibility check: A1 fires slightly fewer but hits slightly more often, so the posterior should be very close to 1/2 and just above it. 21/41 = 0.512 fits; 6/19 = 0.32 does not.
solution: Cannon A1 fires 9 projectiles in the time A2 fires 10, so a randomly chosen projectile comes from A1 with probability 9/19 and from A2 with probability 10/19.
The hit probabilities are P(strike | A1) = 7/10 = 0.7 and P(strike | A2) = 6/10 = 0.6.
Hence option (b) is correct.

tips: Set out the two branches before computing: treated (0.05, recovery 0.50) and untreated (0.95, recovery 0.30). Bayes is then pure arithmetic.
A small prior is rarely overturned by a modest likelihood gain: 5% prior with only a 5/3 likelihood ratio can only reach about 8%. That intuition eliminates options (c) and (d) instantly.
Option (a) 0.03 is the JOINT probability 0.025 rounded - the classic error of forgetting to divide by the total.
Denominator check: 0.025 + 0.285 = 0.310 is the overall recovery rate, 31%, which sensibly sits just above the untreated rate of 30%.
solution: Let T be the event that the patient received the new treatment and R the event of recovery.
Joint probabilities: P(T and R) = 0.05 x 0.50 = 0.025 and P(not T and R) = 0.95 x 0.30 = 0.285.
Total probability of recovery: P(R) = 0.025 + 0.285 = 0.310.
By Bayes' theorem, P(T | R) = 0.025/0.310 = 0.0806.
Rounding, the probability is about 0.08, option (b).

2019-Q14.shortcut: Take absolute values first: |X| = 1.5, 1, 2.5, 3 with the same probabilities 1/6, 1/4, 1/2, 1/12. The products are 0.25, 0.25, 1.25, 0.25, summing to 2.
tips: E(|X|) is NOT |E(X)| - apply the absolute value to each value before weighting. Here E(X) = 0.75 while E|X| = 2.
Convert to twelfths at the start: the probabilities are 2/12, 3/12, 6/12, 1/12, which also verifies that they sum to 1.
The arithmetic is unusually friendly: three of the four products equal 0.25 and the fourth is 1.25, so the total 2 falls out at a glance.
Option (b) 1/4 is the value of a single term and option (c) 3/2 comes from mishandling the largest-probability term - both punish partial arithmetic.
solution: The random variable takes the values -1.5, -1, 2.5, 3 with probabilities 1/6, 1/4, 1/2, 1/12. These sum to 2/12 + 3/12 + 6/12 + 1/12 = 1, so the distribution is valid.
The absolute values are |X| = 1.5, 1, 2.5, 3 with the same respective probabilities.
Hence E(|X|) = 2, option (d).

2019-Q15.shortcut: The 7th child is the 2nd daughter means exactly 1 daughter among the first 6, then a daughter. P = C(6,1)(1/2)^6 x (1/2) = 6/128 = 3/64.
tips: This is the negative binomial pattern: P(the rth success occurs on trial n) = C(n-1, r-1) p^r q^(n-r). Here n = 7, r = 2, p = 1/2, giving C(6,1)(1/2)^7 = 6/128.
Do not use the plain binomial C(7,2)(1/2)^7 = 21/128 - that answers 'exactly 2 daughters in 7 children', which is planted as option (c) in the equivalent 21/64 form.
The last trial is FIXED as a success, so the combination is chosen from n - 1 = 6 trials, not from 7. That single distinction is what the item tests.
6/128 must be reduced to 3/64 to match the options; always reduce before comparing.
solution: Let a 'success' be the birth of a daughter, with p = 0.5 for each child independently.
The event is that the 2nd daughter arrives exactly on the 7th child. This requires exactly 1 daughter among the first 6 children, and then a daughter on the 7th.
P(exactly 1 daughter in 6 children) = C(6,1)(0.5)^1(0.5)^5 = 6 (0.5)^6 = 6/64.
P(7th child is a daughter) = 0.5, independently of the first six.
Hence option (a) is correct.

2019-Q16.shortcut: Y = X^2 + 3 is one-to-one on the non-negative integers, so X = sqrt(y - 3) and the support is y = 3, 4, 7, 12, 19, ... Substituting k = sqrt(y-3) into the Poisson pmf gives option (a).
tips: For a strictly monotone transformation of a DISCRETE variable, simply invert: P(Y = y) = P(X = g^(-1)(y)). No Jacobian is ever involved for discrete variables.
Build the support explicitly from k = 0, 1, 2, 3: y = 3, 4, 7, 12. Options (c) and (d) omit y = 3 (the image of k = 0) and are eliminated at once.
Options (b), (c) and (d) also contain sqrt(3 - y) or a negative exponent, both of which are undefined or wrong for y > 3 - a sign check alone finishes the item.
The source prints the factorial as sqrt((y-3)!) where (sqrt(y-3))! is meant; the intended reading is k! with k = sqrt(y-3). Read past the typography and match on the support and the exponent.
solution: X is Poisson with P(X = k) = e^(-lambda) lambda^k / k! for k = 0, 1, 2, ...
The transformation Y = X^2 + 3 is strictly increasing on the non-negative integers, so it is one-to-one there and can be inverted: X = sqrt(Y - 3).
The support of Y is obtained from k = 0, 1, 2, 3, ...: y = 0 + 3 = 3, 1 + 3 = 4, 4 + 3 = 7, 9 + 3 = 12, and so on, i.e. y in {3, 4, 7, 12, 19, ...}.
For each such y, P(Y = y) = P(X = sqrt(y - 3)) = e^(-lambda) lambda^(sqrt(y-3)) / (sqrt(y-3))!.
Options (c) and (d) exclude y = 3 from the support and use sqrt(3 - y), which is not real for y > 3; option (b) uses a negative exponent on lambda. All three are inadmissible.
Option (a) has the correct support and the correct exponent sqrt(y-3), so it is the intended key.

2019-Q17.shortcut: The number of weekly tickets until the first win is geometric on {1, 2, 3, ...}, whose mean is 1/p.
tips: Two geometric means to keep apart: counting TRIALS until the first success gives 1/p; counting FAILURES before it gives q/p = 1/p - 1 (option b).
The phrase 'until he wins' includes the winning week itself, so the trial-counting version applies.
Intuition check: if p = 1/50 you expect about 50 weeks, which is 1/p. If the answer were 1/(1-p) it would be barely more than 1 week - clearly wrong.
Options (c) and (d) use 1 - p in place of p and correspond to counting until the first LOSS, a different experiment altogether.
solution: Each week the person buys one ticket, winning with probability p independently of other weeks.
Let X be the number of weeks up to and including the first win. Then P(X = k) = (1-p)^(k-1) p for k = 1, 2, 3, ...
This is the geometric distribution on the positive integers.
Its expectation is E(X) = sum over k >= 1 of k (1-p)^(k-1) p = p . 1/p^2 = 1/p.
Hence the expected number of weeks required is 1/p.
Option (a) is correct.

2019-Q18.shortcut: Statement 4 fails at once (sums of binomials are binomial only when p is common), and statement 1 gives a^2/(a-b)^2 = 1/p^2, not generally an integer. Statements 2 and 3 both check out, so the answer is 2 and 3 only.
tips: Recover n and p from mean and variance: p = 1 - b/a and n = a/p. For statement 2, a = 3.5 and b = 1.75 give p = 0.5 and n = 7; for statement 3, a = 4 and b = 4/3 give p = 2/3 and n = 6.
Bimodality test: the binomial is bimodal exactly when (n+1)p is an INTEGER, the modes being (n+1)p and (n+1)p - 1. Here (7+1)(0.5) = 4, so modes 3 and 4. Statement 2 is true.
For statement 1, note a - b = np - npq = np^2, so a^2/(a-b)^2 = (np)^2/(np^2)^2 = 1/p^2. It is a^2/(a-b) that equals n and is an integer - the squared denominator as printed makes the claim false.
Sums of independent binomials add only when the success probability is shared: B(m,p) + B(n,p) = B(m+n,p). With different p the sum is not binomial, which kills statement 4 and options (b) and (d).
solution: Write a = np and b = npq for the binomial mean and variance, so a - b = np - npq = np(1 - q) = np^2.
Statement 1: a^2/(a-b)^2 = (np)^2/(np^2)^2 = n^2 p^2/(n^2 p^4) = 1/p^2, which is not an integer for general p (it is a^2/(a-b) that equals n). FALSE.
Statement 2: a = 3.5, b = 1.75 give q = b/a = 0.5, so p = 0.5 and n = a/p = 7. Since (n+1)p = 8(0.5) = 4 is an integer, the distribution has two modes, 3 and 4 - it is bimodal. TRUE.
Statement 4: if X ~ B(m, p1) and Y ~ B(n, p2) are independent, X + Y is binomial only when p1 = p2. In general it is not. FALSE.
Only statements 2 and 3 are correct, option (c).

2019-Q19.shortcut: A linear change of scale multiplies the covariance by a and the standard deviation by |a|, so the correlation is multiplied by a/|a| - the SIGN of a. Hence r(X,Z) = (a/|a|) r.
tips: Rule: correlation is unchanged by a shift, and under scaling it is multiplied by the sign of the multiplier. The magnitude |r| never changes.
Option (a) is right only when a > 0; the question allows any non-zero a, so the sign factor must appear explicitly.
Option (b) r|a| is dimensionally impossible - a correlation is bounded by 1, but r|a| could exceed 1 for large a.
Option (c) uses |r| and so loses the original sign of r; only option (d) preserves r's own sign while applying the sign of a.
solution: Let Z = aY + b with a not equal to 0.
Covariance: Cov(X, Z) = Cov(X, aY + b) = a Cov(X, Y).
Standard deviation: sd(Z) = |a| sd(Y), since the constant b shifts but does not scale.
Therefore r(X, Z) = a Cov(X,Y) / [sd(X) . |a| sd(Y)] = (a/|a|) . Cov(X,Y)/(sd(X) sd(Y)) = (a/|a|) r.
So the correlation keeps its magnitude |r| and takes the sign of a times the sign of r.
Hence option (d) is correct.

2019-Q20.shortcut: Integrate out y: the integral of 4xy dy from 0 to 1 is 4x(1/2) = 2x. So f_X(x) = 2x on [0,1].
tips: Marginal of X = integrate the joint density over ALL values of y. Here the y-integral of y over (0,1) is 1/2, so the factor 4 halves to 2.
Normalisation check: the integral of 2x over (0,1) is 1, confirming a valid density. Option (a) integrates to 2 and option (c) to 1/4, so both are invalid densities and can be struck out immediately.
The joint density factorises as (2x)(2y), so X and Y are independent Beta(2,1) variables - recognising the product form gives both marginals at once.
Whenever the options are proportional to one another, use the 'integrates to 1' test - it decides the question faster than doing the integral.
solution: The joint density is f(x, y) = 4xy on the unit square 0 <= x <= 1, 0 <= y <= 1.
The marginal density of X is f_X(x) = integral over y from 0 to 1 of 4xy dy = 4x [y^2/2] from 0 to 1 = 4x (1/2) = 2x.
So f_X(x) = 2x for 0 <= x <= 1.
Check: the integral of 2x from 0 to 1 is [x^2] from 0 to 1 = 1, a valid density.
Hence option (b) is correct.
